en: The *Candana-vṛkṣa-sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, now appended to the Han Records.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying with a community of bhikṣus in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, at the place called Kāla...
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada reverently honored the Buddha’s sublime Dharma and invited the Buddha for offerings.
When the Buddha had finished his benediction, the householder stood solemnly before the Buddha, wishing to hear the meaning of the Dharma.
The Buddha then smiled, and light of five colors issued from his mouth, circled his body three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; when he smiles, he will surely preach the Dharma to deliver and liberate those who are to be saved."
"I pray that you will explain it for me!
The World-Honored One said, "Excellent, Ānanda!"
With vast compassion, I wish to open up the bridge of Dharma for all beings.
As for the deportment of a śramaṇa, you should conform to its model;
I shall now expound it—listen attentively and take it to heart.
In that country, five hundred men went to sea to gather treasures. Having disembarked their ship and returned by land, they passed through deep mountains and halted for the night at sunset.

They prepared their gear early for departure; four hundred and ninety-nine men led the way and departed, while one man, having fallen asleep, lost his companions. He then encountered falling snow and rain from the heavens, losing his path and becoming stranded in the midst of the mountains in dire distress, weeping and crying out to Heaven.
There was a great sandalwood tree, and the tree spirit said to the poor man, "You may stay here;
we shall provide for your clothing and food among ourselves, and you may depart when spring arrives."
The destitute man remained there for three months and addressed the tree deity, saying:

"Having received your grace, I have been spared my life and limb; yet I have not yet offered even a small token of gratitude. Looking back, I have my two parents who remain in their native land, and I truly long to return. I pray that you will grant me leave to depart!"
The tree spirit said,
"Excellent! and,
acting according to his own wish, he bestowed upon him a single ingot of gold.
"Not far from here you shall find a kingdom and a city, where you may return to your own village.
As the poor man was about to depart, he asked the deity, "This tree is fragrant and pure, a rarity in this world; as I am now about to leave it behind, I pray that you tell me its name!"
The spirit said,
"There is no need to ask!
The destitute man spoke again:
"Relying on this tree for three months, I am now about to depart and return home with a heart full of resentment.
When I reach my own country, I shall proclaim the kindness of this tree!"
The spirit then said:
"This tree is named candana; its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves cure a hundred ailments of man. Its fragrance is heard from afar; it is a marvel of the world."
"What people greedily seek after need not involve the Way!
Later, when the destitute man returned to his native country, his relatives both inside and outside the family welcomed him with joy and merriment.
Not long thereafter, the king fell ill with a headache; he offered prayers to Heaven and Earth, as well as to the spirits of the mountains and rivers, yet his illness did not subside.
A skilled physician examined him and declared that he could only be protected by *candana* sandalwood; only then would his illness be cured.

The king immediately sought it among the common people, but none was to be found. He then issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom, promising that whoever obtained *candana* sandalwood would be enfeoffed as a marquis and given the king’s younger daughter in marriage.
At that time, the poor man, hearing that the reward for the tribute was substantial, went to the king's presence and said,
"I know the location of the sandalwood!
The king then ordered an attendant official to take the poor man to go and harvest the sandalwood trees.

Upon arriving at the tree, the messenger saw that it was tall and straight, with luxuriant branches and foliage, its flowers and fruits resplendent, such as were rarely seen by men; his heart could not bear to cut it down.
If he does not attack, he violates the king’s command and his illness will not be cured;
if he attacks, his heart feels a deep, lingering ache.
He hesitates and ponders, not knowing what to do.
The tree spirit then spoke from mid-air:
"Cut it down, but leave its roots!
Once it has been cut, smear it with human blood and cover it with livers and intestines; the tree will naturally grow back, restored to its former state."
Having heard these words from the spirit, the messenger immediately ordered men to cut it down.
A poor man was staying by the side of the tree; as the tree fell to the ground, its branches struck and killed the poor man.
The messenger then deliberated with his attendants, saying:
"Just now the tree spirit said:
'One must obtain human blood, liver, and intestines to offer as a sacrifice to the tree.'"
His heart was despondent, not knowing with whom he should fill this [debt].
"Now that this man has died, let him serve as the substitute," he thought,
and then he butchered him and took his liver and blood.
Just as the deity had commanded, the tree grew back immediately.
The king loaded the felled trees onto a carriage and returned to his kingdom; the physician then administered the medicine, and the king’s illness was cured, bringing joy to the entire nation.

The king commanded the people of the kingdom that all who were ill should go to the palace gate; the king would come forth and provide them with fragrant medicines, so that all their illnesses were cured.
The king’s own person was healthy and at peace, and the common people were free from disease; the entire nation rejoiced, and thus it attained an era of great tranquility.
Ānanda withdrew to sit down, bowed his head in prostration, and asked with earnest words:
"How can this pauper be so devoid of gratitude as to violate the tree spirit’s solemn words and oath?
The Buddha replied:
"In the distant past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a family of three: a father and his two sons.
The father upheld the five precepts, practiced the ten wholesome deeds, and observed the eightfold fast without ever being remiss;
the eldest son constantly burned incense in the air within the central courtyard to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions."
"I am a foolish younger brother, ignorant of the Three Honored Ones, and have thus carelessly covered the incense with my robe.
His elder brother said to him:
"This is a matter of great gravity; why did you commit this transgression?"
The younger brother gave rise to an evil intention, vowing to sever his elder brother's two feet;
the elder brother likewise conceived the thought that he would strike and kill his younger brother.
Their father said:
"The two of you, my sons, have been quarreling and have caused me a headache.
The elder son replied,
"I pray that my body may be broken to serve as medicine, so that my father's illness may be relieved."
"One must not speak falsely with the mouth; therefore, one suffers punishment life after life.
My younger brother conceived an evil intent, wishing to cut off my elder brother's feet, and later indeed led men there to cut down the tree."
The elder brother wished to strike his younger brother to death; now having become a tree spirit, he indeed used the tree as his body to strike and kill his brother.
As for the king who suffered from a headache at that time, he was [the younger brother's] father; because he observed the precepts with diligent vigor, he attained such noble status.
At that time, he said, "May this cause me a headache," and later he indeed suffered from a headache; each received their own retribution.
The Buddha said, "The retribution for sin and merit follows one like a shadow follows a form."

The Buddha extensively expounded for him the precepts of body, speech, and mind; the householder then attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. Leading his wife and children, he offered his family wealth to the Buddha, and each of them made vows for the Path.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the householder rejoiced and paid homage.
This concludes the *Candana-vṛkṣa-sūtra* preached by the Buddha.
